text: The first time you present to a real review board, the questions feel like they could come from anywhere. In practice, an experienced reviewer's questions cluster into a small number of recurring categories, because their job is to probe the same handful of failure classes in every design they look at. Learn those categories and the meeting stops feeling unpredictable.

Four categories cover almost everything. 'What happens when X fails' is the resilience question from Chapter 4, aimed at your specific design — pick the component most likely to break and ask it yourself first. 'What does this cost at 10x scale' catches designs that look fine at pilot volume but hide a cost curve that bends badly once a tier boundary or egress charge kicks in. 'What's the security blast radius' is the account-boundary question from Chapter 2 — what else is reachable if this one piece is compromised. And 'what's the simplest version of this' is a sincere question about ongoing complexity cost, not an attack on your design's sophistication.

The way to walk in prepared is to run the failure question on yourself before anyone else asks it — a pre-mortem, component by component: how it fails, what else it takes down with it, and what the mitigation actually is. Do that exercise with your own team before the real review, and the board's version of the same question stops being a surprise.

Beyond the pre-mortem, know your numbers cold: the unit cost per request or per user, where that cost curve has a cliff rather than a smooth slope, and roughly what scale factor breaks the design's current assumptions. Keep the deep detail — a full cost breakdown, a subnet-level network diagram — in appendix slides outside the main deck, so the presentation stays tight but the answer is one click away the moment it's asked.

Anticipating these four categories doesn't make every tradeoff in your design disappear — it just means you walk in already knowing where the hard questions will land. Next lesson is about what happens once one of those hard questions lands squarely on a tradeoff you made on purpose: how to defend it with the reasoning behind it, instead of getting defensive about it.
